A summer drought, followed by flooding, had killed the root structures that mushrooms grow from, experts revealed.
Marlow Renton, of Hereford-based Wild Food UK, one of Britain’s leading foraging experts, said: “This summer, fungi have come under attack from two fronts – the drought, which is really bad for the mycelium, [the root-like body that grows underground] and then flooding, which also kills the mycelium.
“Some fungi, like chicken of the woods – Laetiporus sulphureus – have done quite well this summer but the mycorrhizal fungi – penny buns, chanterelles, morels and milk caps – that rely on the health of their tree partners have really suffered because they need moisture in the ground.
“This moisture feeds the trees and the trees provide nutrients for the fungi. When the ground is hot and dry, it has a devastating effect on the mycelium which shrinks back and dies.”
Mr Renton revealed porcini are not growing where he can usually find them, saying: “Where we would normally have a lot of penny buns at this time of year, I’ve only found one. You would normally see them around late August and all through September.”
Mr Renton, who has run foraging courses for 15 years, said he expects the fungi to start fruiting by October, but these are then at risk from frost. Because of the late growth spurt, the total mass of fungus fruit would be lower than normal, he said.
Dr Carol Verheecke-Vaessen, a senior lecturer in applied molecular mycology at Cranfield University, blamed climate change.
She said: “This summer was the hottest on record for the UK and third driest July on record, [with the] driest July on record for England. Such climatic changes, combining hot and dry conditions, impact the soil moisture that may lead to delayed or reduced production of fungal fruiting bodies – the visible reproductive structure also known as ‘mushroom’ harvested in the wild.
“It is especially relevant to species sensitive to temperature and drought. Evidence in the UK shows that fruiting dates in southern England are extending.”
Commercial mushroom growers have also been affected by the heatwave, because their growing tunnels became too hot for mushrooms to grow.
Adrian Ogden, of Gourmet Woodland Mushrooms near Leeds, runs a laboratory that supplies mushroom spores to growers – including black morels, shiitake and oyster mushroom varieties. He was forced to close for two weeks during the summer because the spores would not survive being transported in the searing heat.
He said: “I have been doing this for 26 years and this is the most challenging year I have ever had. Smaller growers that don’t have the expensive air conditioning the larger growers use really struggled in the heatwave as they grow their fungi in tunnel-like environments.
“The temperatures got so high that many mushroom (growing) bags wouldn’t produce – the same issue that we have seen occurring in the UK countryside.
“If it’s too hot the mycelium, which underpins the fruiting process stays vegetative as it needs cool temperatures to shift into its reproductive stage.
“I had to close for two weeks and now I am facing installing expensive new air conditioning in case of future heatwaves.”

CM Vishnu Deo Sai Surveys Flood-Hit Bastar, Reviews Relief Measures
Sep 28th, 2026 10:00 pm |
By ThenewsmanofIndia.com |
Category: LATEST NEWS
Chhattisgarh Chief Minister Vishnu Deo Sai conducted an aerial survey of flood-affected areas in Bastar and reviewed the situation arising from heavy rains and flooding in the region. He was accompanied by Principal Secretary Subodh Kumar Singh during the assessment.
In Jagdalpur, the Chief Minister inspected flood-affected areas and interacted with affected citizens to understand their difficulties and the assistance required. He also reviewed arrangements at relief camps and directed officials to ensure that essential assistance reaches every affected family without delay.
Later, during his visit to Sukma district, Sai met flood-affected families and visited relief camps to assess the arrangements and understand the challenges being faced by residents.
The Chief Minister directed the administration to address the problems of affected people on priority and ensure that relief and essential facilities reach them in a timely manner. He said the safety and well-being of every flood-affected citizen remains the state government’s priority during the crisis.
